decisions.quote: We tested the precise model developed in the original report. This model provided a small improvement in the prediction of treatment response. It explained an additional 2% of the variance beyond baseline symptom severity, which attained marginal statistical significance and was approximately 1/10th of the effect size in the original report. A more flexible test of model replication, which used the amygdala connectivity target regions from the original report and estimated model parameters on the replication dataset, found no significant prediction of treatment response. Overall, our results support the hypothesis that some features of the amygdala might predict treatment response in SAD, but that more strongly predictive models must be developed for scientific and clinical applications.
decisions.reason: The authors do not conclude that the replication failed outright; instead, they report that the precise original model positively predicted treatment outcomes with a small improvement (2% additional variance explained, p = 0.10, plus close replication of the baseline symptom parameter), whereas a more flexible model replication estimating parameters in the replication dataset and a test in the CBT-immediate subset found no significant prediction of treatment response. Because the paper presents contrasting outcomes across the direct and flexible/subset replication tests and frames the evidence as partial support requiring stronger models, 'mixed' is correct under the codebook.
